title: AI Strategist: Governance and Responsible AI
description: Domain 3 (24%): the six responsible AI dimensions, governance by design, human oversight, accountability, regulation, risk classification, bias, IP and reliability risks.

cards.definition: The six the exam names: fairness, explainability, privacy, safety, transparency and robustness. AWS's own list adds more, such as controllability, veracity and governance.
Building responsible AI and governance into a project from the design stage and across its lifecycle, rather than adding checks just before launch.

example.text: A team planning a claims chatbot runs its risk review and agrees its responsible AI tests at the design stage. The cost comes early but saves rework and damage later.

cards.definition: AWS best-practice guidance in eight focus areas that follow the AI lifecycle, from use case to monitoring; advisory, not a compliance checklist.
Agreed, written rules for which goal wins when objectives clash, such as accuracy vs. coverage, or more false alarms vs. a faster response.

example.text: A fraud team agrees in advance that a faster response is worth a few more false alarms. When the trade-off comes up later, the tenet settles it.

cards.definition: Shrink scope to the minimum viable use case (one domain, region or user group, with restricted inputs and outputs) to keep the value while cutting risk.

example.text: Instead of a general diagnosis assistant, a team launches one that reads only structured lab results for a single condition.

cards.definition: Put people where outputs are hard to judge or errors are costly, and give reviewers explanations and confidence scores to decide well.
Pre-set triggers that send a case to a person, based on alert severity, confidence thresholds and business impact, with clear decision rights.

example.text: An invoice assistant posts routine, low-value invoices automatically. Any exception or large amount is flagged for a person to review.

cards.definition: A board with representatives from many business units (such as legal, HR, procurement, communications, and government and regulatory affairs) that oversees responsible AI and regulatory alignment.
Sets criteria for evaluating foundation models, reviews requests to use them, and checks compliance, working with legal and compliance teams.
A named senior leader answerable for responsible AI outcomes, backed by cross-functional review boards and policy templates; distinct from sponsoring the program or owning a business result.
EU law with a risk-based approach: the higher the risk, the stricter the rules. High-risk uses such as healthcare face duties like human oversight, and some uses are banned outright.
Which laws apply depends on where data is collected and processed and where decisions apply, so name the exact countries and involve legal early.

example.text: A lender builds a credit-scoring tool in one country but will score applicants in three others. Legal reviews each country's rules before the use case is approved.

cards.definition: A voluntary US framework for managing AI risk; AWS advises aligning your own AI risk approach with it and adapting controls for AI-specific risks.
In Amazon Bedrock, your content isn't used to improve the base models or shared with model providers, and it is encrypted in transit and at rest.
Rate each potential harm for likelihood and severity (for example 1 to 5 each) and combine them into a risk level: low, medium, high or critical.
A living record of each AI risk: use case, harmful examples, affected stakeholders, likelihood, severity, risk level and mitigation, kept current.
Set controls by deployment context and user exposure: a public-facing system warrants different controls than an internal one, and safety limits may need to be stricter than security ones.

example.text: A bank uses the same model for a staff summarizer and a public chatbot. The public chatbot gets stricter limits on harmful content and hallucinations.

cards.definition: Ongoing watch over system health, business and user outcomes, model quality, and compliance and risk signals, with alerts and a planned response.
A list of every AI workload in use, approved and shadow, so the organization knows where AI runs before trying to control it.
Bias can enter through the data, the training or the deployed model, so check for it during data preparation, after training and in production.
A deployed model becoming biased over time because live data differs from its training data, so fairness needs ongoing monitoring, not a one-off check.

example.text: A home-price model trained when mortgage rates were low starts to skew once rates change. Ongoing bias monitoring catches the shift.

cards.definition: A buy-or-build factor: AWS defends customers against third-party IP claims over output of listed AWS generative AI services, but not if your inputs infringe or you disable its filters.

cards.term: AI IP risk in both directions
cards.definition: AI can leak your confidential data out and can produce output that infringes others' copyright; ask how each vendor handles both.
Ground answers in trusted documents with RAG, write clear and specific prompts, train on good data, and add guardrails that check outputs.
AWS sorts generative AI use into five scopes, from a public consumer app (1) or enterprise app (2) to building on, fine-tuning or training your own model (3-5); more scope, more you own.
Configurable filters, such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, that block harmful content and denied topics, redact sensitive information and flag likely hallucinations before users see them.
